#9778. Agents Are Not the Answer. Engineering Is.

How to build with rules, skills, hooks and subagents around a coding agent

For a while, I thought the problem was the model.

The agent would put a network call straight inside a screen component, and I would add a sentence to the next request: keep network calls out of the components. It would write a date-formatting helper when one already existed two folders away, and I would add another sentence. The requests got longer. The instructions file got longer. On the days the agent followed all of it, I took that as proof that the setup worked. On the days it followed none of it, I blamed the model.

It took me longer than I would like to admit to do the obvious thing, which was to stop writing and go look at what the tool was actually loading.

The rules I had written with the most care had never been read, not once. Their path patterns expected folder names that were different from the real ones. The instructions file stated a test count that was half the true number, and pointed to a document that didn't exist. In a folder above the project there was an old copy of that same file, loaded together with the new one and contradicting it. And a block I trusted completely had been letting everything through for weeks.

The model had been doing what it could with what I had put in front of it. I had been treating those files as notes to a colleague, when they were software: they had bugs, and I had never tested them.

As I write this, I don't have all the answers about how to make coding agents behave. Probably I never will. Section 9.5 lists what is still unproven, and it is not a short list. But I keep asking questions, and a few of them have turned out to be the right ones. Who decides that this piece comes into play? What happens when it fails? How would a person check?

Coding agents fail less from a lack of model capability than from a lack of engineering around the model. What the agent knows, what it can do and what stops it from making mistakes are all defined by a set of files: permanent instructions, rules per area, skills, subagents, hooks, permissions and memory. This text treats that set as software. It has an architecture, it has typical defects, and it can be tested.

The text is for anyone setting up or maintaining an environment of coding agents, in any tool. The examples use Claude Code's names, but the concepts hold for any tool that reads an instructions file such as AGENTS.md. Section 9 shows all of it applied to a real financial platform, with measured numbers. That is where the story in the prologue comes from.

A coding agent is a language model running in a loop: it reads the request, decides on an action (read a file, run a command, edit), receives the result, and decides on the next one. Everything it knows at that moment is in the context window: the system instructions, the configuration files that were loaded, the conversation, and the tool results. The model has no memory other than what is there and what it learned in training.

There is a useful image for this, attributed to Andrej Karpathy: the model is the processor and the context window is the RAM. Context engineering is deciding what occupies that memory at each step.

Intuition says that giving the model more information helps. It is a reasonable intuition. It is also wrong, or at least wrong past a certain point.

Anthropic describes the phenomenon as context rot: as the window fills up, the model gets worse at retrieving each individual piece of information. Attention is a budget. An important rule buried in a thousand lines of instructions has less effect than the same rule in a file of a hundred.

The practical consequence is the central principle of this text: look for the smallest set of high-signal tokens that produces the behavior you want. Every piece described from here on is a way of applying that principle.

The files that configure an agent have readers (the models). They have behavior (what the agents do because of them). They have bugs (a hook that doesn't fire, a path pattern that doesn't match). And they have debt (a number that stopped being true).

In other words, the practices that apply to product code apply to them as well: one responsibility per file, clear names, nothing duplicated, tests, review and maintenance.

This is the text loaded in every session, for every agent. It holds what is always true: what the project is, the vocabulary of the domain, the real commands, the security rules, the forbidden zones and the definition of done.

Because it enters every context, each line costs attention on every task. The rules for writing it:

A wrong fact in this file costs more than a missing one, because it teaches the model to act with confidence on something false.

Rules are the instructions file sliced by responsibility: one rule for the backend, another for the app, another for tests. A rule can declare which paths it applies to; in that case it is only loaded when a file from that area enters the conversation. A rule with no scope is always loaded, like the main file.

Rules are binding. Write "every new route has an entry in the permissions manifest", not "consider adding one". And name model files: pointing to a well-made file of 44 lines teaches more than describing what a clean route is.

A skill is a folder with an instructions file that has a name and a description. Of all the skills available, the model sees only those two things: name and description. When the task matches a description, it loads the body. This is called progressive disclosure. The knowledge exists, but it only takes up context when it is needed.

That is why the description is the most important part of a skill. It has to say what the skill covers and when to use it, in the words that show up in real requests. A vague description never fires.

Skills hold recipes (how to create a migration), formats (the body of a pull request), catalogs (code smells and their refactorings) and technology knowledge written from the project's real code. A skill can also be invoked by hand, like a command, and can be marked so the model never starts it on its own. That is useful for expensive flows.

A subagent is a role defined in a file: description, allowed tools, model and a system text. When it is called, it runs in a new, empty context window. It receives only the brief the calling agent wrote and the project's instructions files. When it finishes, it hands back a report. Everything it read along the way is thrown out.

The cost is real: the subagent knows nothing about the conversation, and what comes back is a summary. Detail is lost in both directions. Delegating only pays off when the work is large, independent, or needs fresh eyes.

Hooks are scripts the tool executes on events: before a tool call, after it, at the end of a turn. A hook that runs before the call can allow it, deny it or ask for confirmation. A hook that runs after can return text that enters the agent's context.

Hooks are the only piece that doesn't depend on the model obeying. They have two uses:

Rules for hooks: minimal dependencies, errors never silenced, denial messages that say what to do instead, fast execution, and tests with expected allow and deny cases.

Keep that list in mind. Each item on it was learned from something that went wrong, and we will get to those in section 9.3.

Declarative lists of deny, ask and allow, by tool pattern and path pattern. They cover the simple case with no script: never read secret files, always ask before a commit. Whatever needs logic (block an existing migration, allow a new one) goes into a hook.

A directory where the agent writes down facts that should outlive the session: decisions made and the reasons for them, the preferences of whoever works with it, facts about the environment that aren't in the repository. A short index is loaded at the start of each session.

Memory is not a diary. Task state and summaries of finished work stay out, because they age fast and take up context forever.

The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for exposing external tools and data (ticket manager, database, documents) to the agent through a typed interface. It replaces hand-made integrations. Every connected server adds tool descriptions to the context, so the same discipline applies: connect what gets used.

When the description matches, or by command

Birgitta Böckeler, in Context Engineering for Coding Agents, organizes these pieces around one question: who decides that the piece comes into play?

There is a detail here that is easy to miss. Even when loading is guaranteed, obedience is not. A rule in the instructions file is always in the context, and the model can still fail to follow it in a long task. Only hooks and permissions guarantee the effect.

Out of this comes what I consider the most useful design rule in this text:

can be checked by a tool (types, lint, tests)

requires judgment and applies to one kind of task

requires focus, a different permission or fresh eyes

When an agent gets something wrong, the right question is which layer was missing. The fix goes into that layer. One more sentence in the next request fixes nothing.

In Building effective agents, Anthropic recommends starting with the simplest solution and using composed, predictable patterns before handing out open-ended autonomy. There are five patterns:

One design that works well is to have a single agent the person talks to. It answers questions by reading the code, gives opinions, and delegates when the work calls for it. This agent runs as the main session, not as a subagent, and it has the list of specialists it can call.

Three rules keep this design cheap and safe:

The subagent knows only the brief. Nothing else.

Anthropic reports, in How we built our multi-agent research system, that vague briefs made subagents duplicate work, leave gaps or misread the task. A complete brief has:

The report has a fixed format. For a critic: verdict, blocking points, warnings and suggestions, each with file and line. For a builder: files changed, what was removed, commands run and their results, and what could not be done. The fixed format is what makes the flow auditable.

Before calling review, it checks the acceptance criteria in the code itself, runs the verification commands, compares the error counts against the baseline, and goes through the list of changed files looking for anything out of scope. When something fails, the work goes back to the responsible agent with the concrete problem. The limit is three rounds. After that the flow stops and reports.

Systems with several agents spend several times more tokens than a simple conversation. The same Anthropic text reports prototypes that created dozens of subagents for trivial questions.

Orchestration pays for itself on high-value tasks, with independent parts or parts that need separate review. For a one-line fix, it is waste.

The term comes from Kent Beck and was spread by Martin Fowler in Refactoring. A smell is a surface sign of a deeper structural problem. It isn't a bug: the code works. The cost shows up later, when every change gets more expensive and riskier.

The most used catalog groups smells into five families:

Long function, giant file, long parameter list, primitive obsession

Repeated if chain by type, forced inheritance

Duplicated code, a change that requires editing many files

One change becomes ten, and one gets forgotten

Dead code, abstraction for a future that never arrived, a comment that explains confusing code

Skipped layers, a function that lives off another module's data, long access chains

None of these causes is solved by asking the agent to "write clean code". Each one calls for a different piece.

Before writing: show what good looks like and what already exists.

Numeric limits work better than adjectives: a target of 40 lines per function, new files under 400, at most 4 parameters, at most 3 levels of nesting. The layering rule says where each kind of logic lives, which keeps the handler or the screen from accumulating everything.

Right after writing: deterministic feedback.

A hook that runs after each write analyzes the file and returns a list of problems to the agent, with the instruction to fix them or justify them in the report. Ideally this hook runs the project's linter. Where there is no linter, pattern searches cover part of the ground: too many parameters, deep nesting, an empty catch, commented-out code, too much state in one component. This check is approximate and has to be treated that way. It is a warning, not proof.

Before reporting, the builder runs a short self-check on its own diff. Did any function go over the limit? Did I write a block that already existed, and where did I look? Did I add a literal with business meaning? Did any handler or screen gain data access, an HTTP call or a formula? Did I leave anything dead?

In review: fresh eyes and bounded cleanup.

Every task leaves the area it touched cleaner than it found it.

The limit is what makes the rule workable: the cleanup stays inside the files and functions the task already touches, and it is smaller than the task itself. A cleanup bigger than the feature is another task. Without that limit, the agent turns a small fix into a refactoring nobody asked for and nobody can review.

Known security problems stay outside this rule. Fixing them as a side effect of another task mixes together changes that need their own review.

Small functions, names that say what the thing is

Deep modules: simple interface, hidden complexity

A Philosophy of Software Design (Ousterhout)

Thin route with a tested core; subagent with a short description and a fixed report

Characterization tests before touching legacy code

Working Effectively with Legacy Code (Feathers)

First step of the recipe for decomposing large files

Fitness functions: automatic checks of architectural characteristics

Building Evolutionary Architectures (Ford, Parsons and Kua)

The study Configuration Smells in AGENTS.md Files (arXiv 2606.15828) put together the first catalog of these defects from 100 open source repositories with AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md files. According to coverage of the study, at least one defect showed up in 91 of the 100 files, and the three most frequent were:

The study also observes that these defects tend to show up together, and in the company of conflicting instructions.

Putting that catalog together with practice, the checklist looks like this:

"Don't use any", "no console.log" in prose

Configure the linter and run it in a hook or in CI

Count the always-loaded lines, adding up all files

Move recipes to skills and areas to scoped rules

PR format, migration steps in the global file

Ask of each section: does this apply to every task?

Extract into a skill with a precise description

List every instructions file the tool loads, including folders above

A version, count or path that doesn't match the code

Compare against the repository; every measurement has a date

The rule lives in one place and is referenced

Its tools can't be restricted and its trigger can't be described

All the knowledge inside the agent's text

Of the ten, the false guarantee is the one I would single out, because it is the most dangerous. A block that fails in silence gives everyone the feeling of protection. Hooks need tests for the same reason authorization code does.

The most repeated recommendation for coding agents is to give the model a verifiable target. Without one, the agent optimizes for looking right. In order of return:

Measuring the flow closes the loop: how many tasks needed more than one round of correction, which categories of defect the reviewer finds most, how much a task costs. Those numbers say which rule, skill or hook is missing.

A regulated platform for online medical appointments and prescriptions, with two repositories: a TypeScript backend of about 175 thousand lines and a mobile app of about 113 thousand.

An audit was carried out by four agents in parallel, with evidence by file and line. This is what it measured:

The audit's conclusion was about process, not knowledge. The model files proved that the team knew how to do it well. Every new feature had been copied from its nearest neighbor, and nothing stood in the way of that.

It is exactly the condition in which a coding agent makes the problem worse.

The dosage checker doesn't read the code in order to give an opinion. It recalculates the doses independently, with mandatory scenarios, and compares.

This is the part of the case I find most useful, and it is the part that looked worst at the time. There were six mistakes.

Hooks that didn't protect. This is the block from the prologue that let everything through. The original hooks called an interpreter that didn't exist on the machine. The error was silenced, the script exited with success, and everything was allowed. Migration protection did not exist for weeks, and nobody noticed. Lesson: minimal dependencies, errors never swallowed, tests for the hook.

Rules that never loaded. The path patterns expected folder names different from the real ones. The rules were there, written with care, and were not read a single time. Lesson: test the pattern against a real path.

Wrong facts in the instructions file. An outdated framework version, a test count at half the real number, a reference to a document that didn't exist. Lesson: measure and date.

A hook that blocked legitimate work. The pattern looked for the text of a forbidden command anywhere on the line, and it matched a file that merely mentioned the command. Lesson: analyze the structure of the command, not the loose text.

Conflicting instructions. When the checklist from section 6 was applied to the configuration itself, an old copy of the instructions file turned up in a folder above, loaded together with the current one and contradicting it. Lesson: list everything the tool loads, not just what is in the project folder.

Style rules in prose. The backend had no linter, so "no any, no debug logging, no fixed decimal places" went into the text and into a pattern-search hook. This is Lint Leakage, accepted knowingly as a provisional measure. The definitive fix is the linter.

Before this work, the repository had a configuration that looked like protection. Now it has one that has been tested.

This changes the conditions under which code gets written there. The audit in section 9.1 found components of 6 thousand lines because every new feature was copied from its nearest neighbor and nothing stood in the way. Today an agent working in that repository starts from the model files. It receives the map of what already exists before writing its first line. It hears about a function that passed the limit in time to fix it. And it cannot grow the files that were marked as never to grow.

The copying that produced the old code has been cut off at each of the four points from section 5.

Three things come next, in this order: the linter on the backend, CI blocking the merge, and the evaluations of the flow. With them, the same baselines that today say where the code stands will say, task after task, how far it has moved

Order of adoption, from the strongest guarantee to the weakest:

Before creating any new piece, eight questions:

Which layer? Permanent fact, on-demand recipe, isolated role or guarantee?

Does something already cover this? Extend it or reference it.

What is the exact trigger? Test it against a real case.

What are the minimum tools? Who writes and who only reads?

What is the output? A fixed format, with evidence by file and line.

How does a person verify it? Command, baseline, diff.

What happens when it fails? A message that teaches the alternative; a limit on rounds.

What is the date of the measurement, and who maintains it?

There is a scene in Neon Genesis Evangelion that I kept coming back t

For most of the series, everyone treats the Evangelions as giant robots. They have pilots, hangars, launch rails and a maintenance crew. Then one of them tears off its own plating in the middle of a fight, and the head scientist, Ritsuko Akagi, says what the engineers had known all along. The plates were never armor. They are restraints, put there to hold back something that is alive, far stronger than the people who built it, and not fully understood by any of them.

I think this is the most accurate picture I have of what this text describes.

The Eva is not a robot. Nobody at NERV programmed it line by line. They found a way to work with it, and then built everything else around that fact: the plating, the cockpit, the cables, the command room. A language model is in the same position. The engineering in sections 2 to 8 is the plating and the command room.

The cable decides how the fight goes. An Eva runs on an external power cable. When the cable is cut, the internal battery lasts five minutes, and every plan made in the command room starts from that number. That is the context window from section 1. It is the scarce resource, and the design is done around it.

Synchronization is a request. The pilot doesn't steer with levers. The pilot thinks, and the Eva moves, as long as the two are in sync. Some days the sync is high and the machine does exactly what was intended. Some days it barely moves. And a few times it stops listening altogether and acts on its own. That is an instruction: followed most of the time, with no promise about the rest.

The restraints are the guarantee. What NERV could not afford to leave to synchronization, it bolted on. The plating doesn't depend on the pilot being calm or on the Eva agreeing. That is a hook. And the series shows what a restraint that fails looks like, which is the false guarantee from section 6: until the moment it breaks, it looks exactly the same as one that works.

Three computers, one decision. NERV's decisions go through the MAGI, three supercomputers that each hold a different side of the same mind and vote. They exist because a single opinion, however intelligent, inherits its own bias. That is the reviewer from section 2.4, who never saw the implementer's reasoning.

Taking the pilot out is the worst idea in the story. At one point the command decides the pilot is hesitating too much and switches to an autopilot, the Dummy Plug. The Eva finishes the job, and what it does cannot be undone, while the pilot sits inside screaming for it to stop. Section 8 is there for that reason: commit, push, migration and publishing stay with the person.

And when it works, everyone is in it. The operation I like most in the series is the one in which the electricity of the entire country is routed into a single rifle. There is a pilot who shoots and a pilot who holds the shield, engineers on the transformers, operators calling out numbers, a commander who has made the plan, and the three computers giving the odds. The first shot misses. The second one doesn't. It is orchestration, including the cost: you black out a country to stop an Angel, not to fix one line.

What I believe will outlast the tools is the question NERV's engineers had to answer for every part of that machine. Is this something we ask of the pilot, or is this something we bolt on?

Martin Fowler and Kent Beck, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code.

Robert C. Martin, Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship.

John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design.

Michael Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code.

Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons and Patrick Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures.

#9777. Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The package adds public-private cyber responders, an AI-focused team run by the economic ministry, and more leeway to use the government's new active cyber-defense powers.

To read this story in Japanese, please click here (translation by our internal AI tool).

With Japan facing a surge in cyberattacks and breaches, the Japanese government has passed a ¥10 billion ($63 million) emergency cybersecurity package aimed at establishing teams of industry and government experts to quickly respond to attacks and better secure its infrastructure.

The four pillars of the strategy include thoroughly implementing basic cybersecurity measures country-wide, including adopting AI for cyber-defense, strengthening the nation's cyber-investigations capabilities, better supporting the victims of cyberattacks, and partnering with private industry to jointly respond to cyberattacks.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called for the cybersecurity measures to be implemented "promptly and effectively" to enhance the nation's cyber resilience.

"Even at this very moment, incidents of unauthorized access and information leaks continue to occur, significantly affecting people's daily lives and business activities," Takaichi said in a published statement announcing the emergency package on November 6. "Let us mobilize the full resources of the Government to strengthen Japan's overall capabilities to respond to cyberattacks."

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

While AI has aided attackers elsewhere, TrendAI has not established a firm link between the increases and the use of AI by attackers, Ryan Flores, co-lead for threat research at TrendAI, a cybersecurity firm, said in a statement on the threats.

"Cyberattacks are increasing globally, and so are the breaches and data leaks as a result," he said. "While AI might not be directly involved, its ability to help the attackers find targets and automate their operations makes cyberattacks scalable. Organizations need to shrink their cyber exposure and close the vulnerabilities in order to lower the odds of being victimized."

Recent compromises include ransomware attacks on business, such as frozen food giant Nichirei and brewery and food giant Asahi, and data breaches targeting GMO Internet Group. While many of the attacks are criminal in nature, the worry is that the stolen information could be used by other criminal groups and nation-state actors against the Japanese public, says Mihoko Matsubara, chief cybersecurity strategist for Japanese telecom giant NTT.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

"If attackers can collect and aggregate enough personal information, they can build detailed profiles of Japanese citizens, from personal preferences to economic activities," she says. "That data could potentially be used for influence operations against Japan, such as targeted disinformation campaigns to manipulate public opinion or undermine trust in Japanese institutions."

The Japanese government intends to use the emergency funding to pursue four broad initiatives to improve its overall cybersecurity posture. Pointing out that many recent breaches could have been prevented by good hygiene, the government's first initiative is to ensure organizations are implementing basic cybersecurity measures, according to the published Japanese notes of the ministerial meeting.

The second major initiative is to improve investigation and information collection capabilities, allowing better analysis that can then be delivered to the public to better prepare them for attacks. Third, the government will strengthen its response to cyberattacks, establishing international partnerships and implementing active cyber-defense measures. Finally, the government plans to create the capability and infrastructure to support victims so that citizens can recover damages and businesses can remain operational.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

"Accessible consultation points and direct expert support will be expanded so that affected organizations and individuals can connect to support without confusion, and communication to prevent secondary harm will be strengthened," the Japanese notes stated. "Work will also begin on building a nationwide mechanism for flexibly dispatching public- and private-sector specialists."

On October 1, Japan's Active Cyber Defense legislation came into effect, authorizing the police and the Self-Defense Forces (SDF) to take strong measures against any cyberattacks that pose a risk to Japan’s national security.

"Many countries would be keen to learn how quickly Japan could respond to which kind of cyberattacks, and with what level of intensity," says NTT's Matsubara, adding: "This emergency package is ... necessary to translate the law’s framework into practical capabilities across the broader economy, preparing organizations of all sizes to prevent, detect and respond to attacks as they become increasingly likely."

However, the funds are only enough to get started, and more will be necessary to continue Japan's investment in cybersecurity, she says.

"The important aspect about this package is that it recognizes that cybersecurity cannot be left entirely to individual organizations," Matsubara says. "Government assistance, in the form of security assessments and incident response or recovery support, can make a difference."

#9776. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9775. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

One useful technical distinction is that AS2650 is an autonomous system, not a single subnet. For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. That matters when a residential proxy makes traffic look trusted simply because the address falls inside an organization’s announced space. I maintain OnlinTools; our Subnet Calculator can show the network, range, broadcast address and host count for a supplied CIDR prefix, but it cannot establish route origin, physical location, ownership, or compromise.

Interesting how a seemingly ordinary device can turn a trusted network into an access point for someone else’s traffic.

What makes this particularly concerning is that the organization may remain completely unaware of how its own infrastructure is being used. A good reminder that information security also depends on visibility into what is actually happening within a network.

The location detail is what separates this from ordinary proxy noise: AS2650 is a fixed, well-known allocation, so any exit node registered there is either a misconfiguration worth escalating internally or an actual beacon worth watching – there’s no third reading. That Infatica nodes bundled into free apps are the vector fits the broader pattern where the resource being rented out belongs to someone who never knowingly agreed to rent it. The persistent two-week window suggests nobody at the network’s edge was watching egress, which is the cheap fix here.

#9774. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9773. Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The CCP built a Big Data system to scrape reams of information and learn about individuals abroad, to potentially target and exploit them. Think Alice Huang Lite.

The Chinese government is keeping tabs on ethnic Chinese people abroad via an AI-powered Big Data mining program. In some cases, the program is helping the government design influence operations targeting high-ranking individuals in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry.

Since the AI boom began, world leaders have been feeling out how to exploit it to cement their power. While Washington's emphasis has been on shorter-term AI ventures — tracking immigrants and political protestors, identifying social services to cut, etc. — the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has been building something more durable: a data center that facilitates gargantuan Web scraping from social media and other public sources, feeds the results into machine learning algorithms, and outputs actionable intelligence for the apparatchiks in Beijing.

That's according to documents leaked to China watchdog NetAskari. In a report shared with Dark Reading and Sky News UK ahead of publication, NetAskari detailed a program that balances straightforward government PR with unsavory surveillance. Sometimes the data gathering has been designed around Cambridge Analytica-style targeted propaganda campaigns. In more nefarious cases, it has been used to identify individuals in political and economic spheres of interest who might one day make good spies or unwitting assets in spy campaigns.

Related:Malicious Linux Implants Mimic Asian Mail Security Products

"A foreign nation with rather undemocratic tendencies is running an extensive, AI-charged analysis and information-scraping operation to find ways to influence other nations' internal social, economic, and political landscapes," a NetAskari analyst explains in an interview with Dark Reading over Signal. "That this system is particularly aiming at the Chinese diaspora, to see if [foreign citizens] can be used to further these ambitions, even if they might not be aware of it, is rather shocking."

On Nov. 8, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang — one of the few most important people in the most important industry in the world — emailed his staff, admitting to an affair with a newly outed spy. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) agent, Alice Huang, redirected Nvidia semiconductors to China, where they're banned, and translated intelligence from the CEO to the CCP.

While the MSS ran Huang, the United Front Work Department (UFWD) took its own, less dramatic approach to the challenge of breaching Taiwan's semiconductor industry.

The UFWD's main game is influence operations, at home and abroad, according to NetAskari. Its mission includes gauging and shaping media narratives about China abroad, engaging Chinese diaspora communities — to their benefit or detriment, depending on the situation — and, in certain cases, attempting to gain influence over powerful or otherwise useful individuals and organizations in China and abroad.

Related:UAE, Saudi Arabia Face Onslaught of Increasingly Complex Cyberattacks

In this instance, the UFWD appears to have been scoping out ethnic Chinese individuals involved in the semiconductor industry. A leaked report titled "Profiles of Ethnic-Chinese Leading Talent in the Chip Field, Their Circle Characteristics, and Work Recommendations" identifies executives of the Taiwanese AI company Skymizer, high-performing students at a top Taiwanese research university, and an AI research center director at Microsoft, among others, as individuals of note. It then details strategies for getting closer to these VIPs, like "leverage non-official organizations — hometown associations, alumni associations, professional societies — for relationship-building and cooperation."

The system used to generate this report is called the "Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform."

The platform's brain is a 500-square-meter Big Data laboratory at Jinan University in Guangzhou, built to comfortably house rows of server racks and at least 100 employees.

Related:Cybercriminals Hack Brazilian Government Servers to Host Phishing Sites

Basically, it's built to ingest massive amounts of online information about overseas Chinese communities, identify people, relationships, and public sentiments, and convert it all into actionable reports for CCP leadership, according to NetAskari.

Social media provides much of the content. The platform scrapes liberally from platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and X, plus Chinese platforms like Weibo and WeChat. As a rule, the actual scrapers are run on machines located in foreign countries. As with Chinese hacking campaigns more broadly, the machines doing the crimes are also shielded behind rotating proxy networks. The goal of this obfuscation, one leaked document explains, is to “ensure the security of data collection and prevent the collection system from being traced and discovered" by targeted platforms.

The data then makes its way to China for processing. Foreign languages are translated into Chinese, keywords are extracted, and meaningful links are drawn. UFWD then cross-references these data with preexisting records of notable people identified as being involved in the media, sciences, politics, etc., as well as blacklisted and "two-faced people." These two sources feed a "business system" — the layer that seems to draw meaningful connections about public sentiments, the results of influence operations, and more.

Sometimes, the final reports outputted by this multitiered system simply concern public relations trends. Sometimes they've been used to identify ethnic Chinese individuals of note around the world — be they Taiwanese engineers, social media influencers, or something in between — and unearth strategies for how to utilize them to further the ends of the Chinese Communist Party.

Overall, the NetAskari analyst describes the Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform as "a worldwide dragnet that uses open source intelligence (OSINT) and Big Data analysis to identify and find potential collaborators, partners, and affiliates that the UFWD can work with to further their goal [of] extending the Communist Party's influence abroad and creating a 'China-friendly' environment in other nations' political, economic, and social settings."

It's nothing the UFWD wasn't doing before, to be sure. Instead, the analyst adds, "What used to be done manually, at a much slower speed, is now supercharged via AI and modern technology."

That, ultimately, is the rub. The leaked documents contain only outdated references, from 2021, about how machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) algorithms fit into this picture. It's unclear whether, and how, more modern large language models have been incorporated into — and potentially supercharged — the system. The better the AI gets, the more wide-ranging and granular the Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform can become, with real consequences for people who may not know they are being targeted by a foreign nation.

"A surveillance state can't accept that its own citizens are escaping to other nations, outside the reach of Beijing's grasp. For the best part of the last 20 years, most people had the luxury to ignore this part of the Chinese state. Often practical and physical limitations restricted Chinese organiations to expand too quickly abroad or even get a foothold. But with remote methods like the ones we have seen applied in the Big-Data center of Jinan University, these 'natural boundaries' don't apply anymore," the analyst laments.

"Pair it now with ever-growing globalization, China's stepping out onto the world stage, and crises of democracy in many Western nations, and it is not hard to see why such operations should concern even average citizens in the US or Europe," he says. "Even if they have no personal ties to China."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9772. Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities

Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

#9771. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.
